The Financial Analyst Memo: every financial table and model output behind this memo

Addtech: a dependable 10% compounder priced for 12%, whose return now turns on the multiple, not the earnings

Addtech (ADDT.B-SE): investment memo. Investment Analyst, 19 November 2026.

Share price SEK 316.20 (3 November 2026). Addtech's fiscal year ends on 31 March, so FY2027 is the year to March 2027. Money is in SEK millions unless stated. The EPS basis, sources and other conventions are set out in the end notes.

#0Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The case in one paragraph. Addtech is a high-quality, low-risk compounder whose EPS should grow about 10% a year, but today's share price implies EPS growth of about 12% a year. At present, bond yields, not company delivery, set the multiple of every premium Swedish compounder, Addtech included. Three clocks run at different speeds: the business is turning up now; consensus estimates have not yet been rebased to the true size of that upturn; and the multiple moves with yields, outside the company's control. With only the business clock helping, the skew of outcomes for Addtech's shares is not unusually positive today. That skew should improve on a timetable that can be dated, and this memo gives the dates and the tests.

What matters most.

  1. Addtech's earnings are dependable, and slower than its "compounder" label suggests. The model has revenue growing about 8% a year, and EBITDA and EPS about 10% a year, to FY2031. The company's target is 15% a year, and EPS grew 16% a year over the last six years. Every element of the 10% base case rests on something already in the accounts. Addtech is a compounder running at about two-thirds of its stated speed.
  2. Today's share price pays for more than the base case. On my arithmetic (topic #11), today's 26.1 times two-year-forward earnings is what the base case is worth only at a 7.5% required return, or what 12% EPS growth for eight years is worth at 8%. The two-point gap between 10% and 12% growth is about what the announced, funded but undelivered step-up in acquisitions would add. The market is paying for the acquisition capacity; the completed deals have so far come at the old pace.
  3. The return on the shares is a statement about the multiple. At the guideline fair multiple of 21.5 times, the model gives a total return of -2.3% to March 2028 and +11.6% to September 2029. At today's multiple, the same earnings give about 12% a year. Earnings growth and the dividend are worth about 11% to 12% a year in either case; the exit multiple decides the rest.
  4. Consensus has the right level of earnings and the wrong shape. Consensus needs organic growth of 6% to 7% in the second half of FY2027, against my 3% to 4%. It carries no future acquisitions, and it assumes falling interest costs and a flat tax rate. Future deals will add to estimates; weaker organic prints, higher interest and higher tax will subtract. I expect net revisions to be down through the May 2027 report and up from the July 2027 report.
  5. The noise in the next three reports can be known in advance. The 2 February 2027 report is the one clean quarter. The May 2027 report will be distorted downwards: Easter falls in March, the comparison quarter is laden with one-offs, and gross margin is compared with its peak. The July 2027 report will be distorted upwards. An investor who waits for "two consecutive quarters of 3% organic growth" will get a false negative in May.
  6. The upside option is real, funded and visible in real time. About SEK 4bn of balance-sheet headroom by FY2028 can fund the 15 to 20 deals a year that management says it can do. Each extra SEK 1bn a year of acquisitions adds about 2.5 to 3 points to EPS growth. Deal flow has quickened in the last seven weeks, with three United Kingdom acquisitions, but that quickening takes the FY2027 pace only to the top of the range of recent years, not above it.
  7. The risk lies in the multiple and in trust, not in the earnings. The likely range of EPS outcomes over 18 months is about -12% to +7% around the base case. The two-year-forward multiple has ranged from 20 to 45 times in five years. The trust risks are a control failure in a group with no internal audit function, and earn-out write-backs that have risen several-fold.
  8. The skew of outcomes turns positive when any two of four conditions hold:
The five judgements that move the value most over one to two years are, in order: the exit multiple; the size and timing of organic growth; the pace and price of acquisitions; the margin path through the wave of input-cost inflation; and the lines below EBITA (interest, tax and the krona). Topic #9 gives the arithmetic for each judgement.

Scorecard

#1Operating environment: tailwinds and headwinds

Bottom lineThe operating environment is a moderate tailwind for Addtech's earnings and an active headwind for its multiple.

Evidence.

  • The short-cycle industrial upturn is real, and Addtech is late to it. The weighted Swedish and euro-area manufacturing index has been above 53 since June 2026, and Addtech's organic growth has historically accelerated two to five quarters after such a rise. Peers in the same niches have already reported the acceleration in organic growth; Addtech reported 2%, although its order intake has exceeded sales for two quarters.
  • A structural layer of demand, a quarter to a third of revenue, has a direction visible for years and a lumpy timing. The layer covers grid, defence, data-centre and electrification customers. Svenska Kraftnät, the Swedish grid operator, plans SEK 225bn of investment over 2026 to 2035, with annual spending planned to step up sharply in 2026 and 2027, and National Grid's capital investment is up 33%. Against that, permits, contractor capacity and installation delays at Vestas (the largest customer of the Energy business area) keep pushing deliveries later.
  • Two drags, sawmill equipment and Nordic construction, are bottoming but not yet recovering.
  • Interest rates turned against the sector in October and November 2026. The Riksbank has raised its policy rate to 2.0%, and a further rise is expected in February. The market prices two to three European Central Bank rate rises by July 2027. Euro-area inflation is 4%, and Brent crude is near USD 115 a barrel.

Inference. The operating environment has moved from headwind to modest tailwind, and it supports organic growth of 3% to 4% almost by arithmetic. The Energy and Industry business areas, a little over a third of sales, shrank about 3% in the first half against exceptional comparisons. If those two business areas merely move to +2%, group organic growth rises by about 1.8 points with nothing else changing. That arithmetic is why I hold 3% to 4% with more confidence than a year of premature sell-side calls for acceleration would otherwise allow, and why I do not stretch to 6%.

One variable sits on both sides of the case: the energy-led inflation shock. The inflation shock adds 1.5 to 2 points of price to near-term organic growth. The same shock drives the rate rises, the one-to-two-quarter lag in passing higher costs through to customers, and the "hesitation" customers show on large projects. For the equity, the net effect of the inflation shock is negative, because its effect on the discount rate is far larger than its effect on revenue (topic #11).

So what. The test of "strong tailwinds and an absence of headwinds" is half met. The operating tailwinds are moderate and improving; the headwind sits on the valuation side and is active.

Against the market. The sell-side narrative ("Buckle up for growth acceleration", DNB Carnegie, 23 October 2026) and I agree on the direction of organic growth. I differ on its size and timing: brokers have applied the two-to-five-quarter lag rule too early for a year, and part of today's order strength is precautionary buying and price rather than volume.

Strongest counter-case

The last time the manufacturing index held between 53 and 59 (2010 to 2012), Addtech's organic growth averaged about 10% for six quarters. Peers show that double-digit organic growth is available now. If restocking stacks on top of real end-demand, consensus is right and my forecast is too low; I put the probability of that outcome at about one in four.

What would change my view

Organic growth of 5% or more in the 2 February 2027 report, with Energy sales clearly up; or, in the other direction, the manufacturing index falling back below 50.

Conclusion: the operating environment is a moderate, improving tailwind worth 3% to 4% organic growth, set against an active rate headwind that bears on the multiple far more than on the earnings.

Score: 61, set by the Rater. The external forces are a moderate, improving net positive on the business itself: a manufacturing index above 53 since June with Addtech's organic growth lagging peers by its usual two to five quarters, a structural grid, defence and data-centre layer on a quarter to a third of revenue (slipping in timing), 1.5 to 2 points of price, and two drags (sawmills, Nordic construction) bottoming. Together they support 3% to 4% organic growth rather than 6%. The rate rise acts mainly on the multiple and is scored in topics 9 and 11, not here. That is an ordinary partial positive, in line with the group's 60: above OEM International's mostly-M&A recovery and below Linea Directa's stronger but more advanced pricing cycle.

#2Internally driven change

Bottom lineThe margin and mix gains are banked; the faster acquisition engine is funded and visible, but not yet delivered.

Evidence.

  • The new group structure is built for more deals. Since October 2025 Addtech has had six business areas and fifteen business units, and each unit head owns a pipeline of acquisition targets. The chief financial officer says the new structure supports 15 to 20 acquisitions a year, up from 10 to 15.
  • Deal delivery so far is at the old pace. Addtech made twelve acquisitions in FY2025, nine in FY2026 and seven so far in FY2027, the seven with about SEK 0.9bn of combined annual sales. Three of the seven are United Kingdom acquisitions made in the last seven weeks (on 2 and 22 October, and Hardall International on 16 November, with about GBP 13m of sales). Annualised, the FY2027 pace is about eleven deals and SEK 1.5bn of acquired sales: the top of the range of recent years, not above it.
  • The mix ratchet works: acquisitions keep lifting the share of higher-margin sales. Proprietary and customised products are about two-thirds of sales, and eight of the nine FY2026 acquisitions were outside the Nordics, where targets carry higher margins. Gross margin rose through eleven quarters of flat volume.
  • Restructuring has paid. The Automation business area's margin rose from 10.5% to 13.7% in the first half of FY2027, with EBITA up more than 50% in both quarters. Capacity that four subsidiaries (about 10% of revenue) added at the trough is now dropping through to profit.
  • Four negatives arrived together in the September quarter. First, earn-out write-backs (gains booked when an acquired company misses the targets on which its deferred purchase payment depended) were about SEK 80m in the first half alone: as much as in all of FY2026, against SEK 10m to 25m a year before that. Second, first-half operating cash flow was flat while EBITA rose 14%. Third, the year-on-year gain in gross margin has halved. Fourth, no financial target has been raised, even though profit over working capital is 82% against a 45% floor.

Inference. Addtech's internal change is the scaling of a proven machine, not a step change. The most bankable changes are those already in the accounts: the richer mix, the Automation recovery and tighter capital efficiency. The one change investors were told to expect, a faster acquisition engine, is still only a claim about capacity. Precedent counsels patience: Indutrade's chief executive said that Indutrade's equivalent reorganisation would take "several years" to lift deal flow.

The under-noticed signal in the earn-outs. An earn-out write-back means that an acquired company missed the plan on which it was bought. The earn-out structure protected the price Addtech paid, which is its acquisition discipline working. But the rising write-backs also say that recently acquired companies are growing below plan, and those companies enter organic growth twelve months after purchase.

So what. Model a margin gain of 20 to 35 basis points a year and acquired growth of 5% to 6% a year. Treat the acquisition step-up as an option that is funded and can be tracked deal by deal.

Against the marketThe market credits Addtech's claimed deal capacity (DNB Carnegie: Addtech "can double earnings twice in ten years" without more leverage). I credit only the deals completed. On earn-outs, the sell-side strips the write-back gains out each quarter but does not read their rising trend as information about deal quality; I do.
Strongest counter-caseDeal flow is quickening now, higher interest rates keep private equity out of small deals, and management describes the pipeline as well filled. The acquisition step-up may be arriving as I write.
What would change my viewAcquired annual sales above SEK 2bn in a fiscal year, with entry multiples still below 8 times EBITA. Acquired sales, not deal count, is the measure, because fifteen small deals can add less than ten larger ones. In the other direction: a further large earn-out write-back, or a goodwill impairment (Indutrade's 2024 pattern was SEK 411m of write-backs matched by SEK 408m of impairment).

Conclusion: internal change is real but incremental; the margin and mix gains are banked, and the acquisition step-up that would change the growth rate is funded, visible in real time and not yet delivered.

Score: 56, set by the Rater. The banked changes are real but incremental: the mix ratchet, Automation's margin up from 10.5% to 13.7%, and a 15-unit structure built for 15 to 20 deals a year. Against them, the acquisition step-up is still only a capacity claim (seven deals and SEK 0.9bn so far, the old pace), earn-out write-backs are several times their old level and signal acquired cohorts below plan, and first-half cash flow was flat. This is gently positive continuity close to Richard's CVS 55, nudged up by a funded, visible deal option. I keep the group's 54 but lift it two points for that option, which places Addtech a little above Shell's incremental self-help and well below OEM International's EQT-driven change of gear.

#3Industry structure, competitive advantage, financial profile and management

Bottom lineTop-quartile foundations justify a narrow range of earnings outcomes and the cohort's multiple, but not a premium to the cohort.

Evidence.

  • Addtech's product markets are benign. The group operates in thousands of small niches, against family-owned competitors that put margin before volume, and its prices held through a two-year trough in volume. No customer exceeds 2% to 3% of sales, and no supplier exceeds 1%.
  • The diversification across subsidiaries is real but smaller than the headline. The twenty largest subsidiaries are about half of revenue, so the group is nearer to 40 to 50 independent bets than to the "more than 150" companies it reports.
  • Addtech has two kinds of competitive advantage. At subsidiary level, specification, customisation and certification create switching costs that are moderate and slowly widening. At group level, Addtech has an acquisition advantage: about 80% of its deals are sourced bilaterally, its median entry price is 6.8 times EBITA (Indutrade: 8.6), and it has issued no equity in 25 years. By design, the group has no purchasing scale and no network effect.
  • The financial profile is strong on capital and mid-table on margin. Return on capital employed is about 22%, profit over working capital is 82%, net debt is about 1.4 times EBITDA, and free cash flow after leases is about 86% to 96% of the model's net income. The EBITA margin of about 16% trails those of Lifco, Diploma and Lagercrantz.
  • Management is stable, internally grown and aligned with shareholders. The chief executive has run the group since 2018, and in that time has more than doubled revenue while lifting margins. Management pay is tied to profit growth and capital efficiency. The gaps are in disclosure and control: no numerical guidance, no named successor, a board controlled by the founding families, no internal audit function and no separate audit committee.

Inference. Addtech's foundations explain why the range of earnings outcomes is narrow and why a premium to the wider market is deserved. They do not explain a premium to the cohort of Nordic serial acquirers. Those peers share Addtech's structure and runway, and Addtech out-executes them on capital efficiency and deal pricing, not on margin or organic growth. As for "stretching goals", the 15% growth target is stretching only in the sense that it is being missed.

Where the fragility sits. Addtech's fragility sits in the two places where its model must scale: the acquisition market, where at least half a dozen new Nordic acquirers now bid for targets, and the control framework, which the owners choose to keep light.

So what. Foundations of this quality make the base case safe. They also mean that the debate about Addtech is rarely about the business and nearly always about the price paid for it.

Against the market. I agree with the market's current pricing of Addtech at parity with its cohort. In April 2026 Addtech traded at about a 15% premium to its closest peers; it now trades at the cohort's multiple, about 18.5 times FY2028 EBITA against a median of 19 times for proven compounders. Parity is right while Addtech's organic growth lags.

Strongest counter-case. Addtech's organic-growth lag against Lagercrantz may reflect local loss of market share rather than business mix, and the available files cannot disprove that explanation. Size also dilutes: the same number of deals on a group twice as large gives 5% acquired growth, not 7%.

What would change my view. Entry multiples drifting above 8 times EBITA; a control failure; or organic growth still trailing peers two quarters after the Energy and sawmill comparisons have normalised.

Conclusion: the foundations are top-quartile for durability and capital efficiency and mid-table for margin and organic growth, which supports a narrow earnings cone and a cohort multiple, not a premium to it.

Score: 76, set by the Rater. Three of the four parts are strong. Fragmented, margin-first niches with no customer above 3%; a group-level acquisition advantage (80% bilateral, 6.8x EBITA entry, no equity in 25 years) on top of moderate switching-cost moats; and a stable, aligned management with a long record. New capital earns about 11% after tax on day one, against a cost of about 8%, and earnings are highly predictable. The figures agree (ROIC 17%, 87th percentile; ROE 91st; capex 0.8% of sales), but margins are only median (EBITDA 46th percentile; EBITA 16% against Lifco's 23%) and governance is light, with no internal audit. So one part is ordinary, which is the 75 level and coherent with the groups' 66, 66, 74 and 75. That puts it level with Tenaris and below Reply's best-in-class organic growth.

#4Guidance conservatism and the record of delivery and upgrades

Bottom lineEstimates still rise mechanically as deals close, but Addtech's run of earnings beats has stopped for now.

Evidence.

  • Addtech gives no numerical guidance, so there is no guidance to be conservative with. Its one growth target, EBITA growth of more than 15% a year over a business cycle, is about five points above the model's base case. Addtech's formal ambition therefore sits above our forecast, not below it.
  • The 15% target faces a dated cliff. The five-year average growth rate that currently supports the target still contains FY2023's +41%. On my approximate figures, the five-year average falls from about 17% to 18% at the May 2027 report to about 12% at the May 2028 report. At that point the company will be below its target on one-, three- and five-year views at once.
  • Management does not manage expectations down. Its one recent forward statement, capacity for 15 to 20 deals a year, raised expectations.
  • The long record of delivery is excellent. EBITA compounded at about 20% a year from 2001 to FY2024, and Addtech beat consensus EBIT in 12 of 18 years, by an average of 10%.
  • The recent record is thinner. Beats against consensus shrank from about 4% to nil over the last four quarters, and both FY2027 quarters needed earn-out gains to reach consensus. On underlying profit, the run of clean beats ended in the March 2026 quarter.

Inference. Addtech's upgrade engine is real, but it comes from a broker convention, not from company conservatism. Brokers add acquisitions to their forecasts only when the deals complete, so estimates rise about 4% to 5% a year as deals close. The long record of beats was built while brokers excluded deals and under-modelled margins. Today brokers over-model organic growth and under-model interest and tax. The historical base rate of beats therefore overstates the odds of beats in the next two reports.

So what. Of Addtech's "beat and raise" record, the "raise" half continues mechanically as deals close. The "beat" half has stopped for now.

Against the market

The market still reads a beat-and-raise story (DNB Carnegie's July report used those words in its title). I think it is a raise-without-beat story until consensus estimates are rebased.

Strongest counter-case

Bear theses on Addtech have rarely been right over 12 to 24 months, and management's cautious tone ("hesitation", "a couple of quarters") may prove conservative against a turning cycle.

What would change my view

An underlying EBITA beat on 2 February with no earn-out gain in it. A raise of the target for profit over working capital (I put the odds at about 30% at the May 2027 report) would signal confidence, but would carry no earnings content.

Conclusion: the conservatism in this case comes from how brokers model acquisitions, not from the company, and for the next two reports that structural tailwind to estimates is offset by a near-year bar that is not low.

Score: 50, set by the Rater. There is no numerical guidance (neutral), and the 15% EBITA target sits about five points above the base and will visibly lapse by May 2028. The long record is excellent (12 beats in 18 years), but over the last two to three years beats shrank from about 4% to nil, both FY2027 quarters needed earn-out gains to reach consensus, and the target has never been raised; the raise in estimates is a broker convention, not company conservatism. Nothing has been missed or cut, so it sits just above the groups' 44 and 45: below CVS's met targets and above Sdiptech's untested ones.

#5Pricing power, operating and financial leverage, cost scope and feedback loops

Bottom lineProfit still grows faster than revenue, but through mix (a ratio of about 1.2) rather than through operating leverage (1.4 in the past).

Evidence.

  • Addtech's pricing power is demonstrated, and its role is changing. Gross margin rose about 330 basis points over 2022 to 2025 on flat volume. From here, price increases add more to revenue (1.5 to 2 points in the near term) and less to margin. The year-on-year gain in gross margin is about to meet last year's peak, and Lagercrantz has just lost 40 basis points of margin to the lag in passing on higher costs.
  • Operating leverage is moderate. Overheads were 11.8% of sales in both FY2023 and FY2026: at low organic growth, the cost base grows with revenue. One point of organic growth is worth about 1.8% of EBITA. The strong drop-through of extra sales to profit is concentrated in the Automation business area, 16% of sales.
  • Financial leverage is low and unused. On my figures, net debt is about 1.3 to 1.4 times EBITDA at March 2027, against an internal ceiling of below 2.0 times. All of Addtech's debt carries floating rates, so one percentage point on interest rates costs about SEK 57m a year after tax (end note 3 covers a query on the model's net debt line).
  • Cost-cutting scope is small by design. Addtech has no central purchasing or shared-service lever, and intends none. Costs flex locally in a downturn (8% of staff left within nine months in 2020), which puts a floor under earnings but is not a source of upside.

The feedback loops.

Above EBITA, the loops reinforce

Addtech buys companies at about 7 times EBITA and is itself valued at about 19 times; each acquisition of a product-owning company lifts the mix; incentives keep working capital tight.

Below EBITA, the loops balance

Amortisation rises 17% in FY2027, interest costs are rising, the tax rate drifts up with the continental mix, and earn-out gains are not assumed to recur.

Inference. The gearing of profit growth to revenue growth has fallen. Over the last six years, revenue growth of 11.6% a year became reported EPS growth of 16.4% a year, a ratio of 1.4. Over the next five years, revenue growth of about 8% becomes EPS growth of about 10%, a ratio of 1.2. The gearing that remains is driven by mix, not by operating leverage, so it is smaller but more reliable.

So what. Outsized profit growth now needs one of two things that the base case does not contain. The first is organic growth above 5%, which would bring back overhead absorption. The second is debt-funded acquisitions, which would put the balance sheet to work. The company holds both options.

Against the market. On margins I agree with consensus: its EBITDA margin path of 18.3%, 18.4% and 18.8% matches ours within 20 basis points. I differ below EBITA, where the leading broker models falling interest costs and a 22.5% tax rate, against the 23.4% already reported and rising.

Strongest counter-case. Addtech's margins have beaten forecasts five years running. A real upcycle would repeat FY2021 to FY2023, when the overhead ratio fell 360 basis points.

What would change my view. The overhead ratio falling below 11.5% with organic growth at 4% or more, which would show that operating leverage is back; or gross margin down year on year for two quarters while input costs rise, which would show that pricing power is straining.

Conclusion: the model still turns revenue growth into faster profit growth, but at a ratio of about 1.2 through mix, not 1.4 through leverage, with the stronger gearing held in reserve as two unexercised options.

Score: 58, set by the Rater. Pricing power is proven (gross margin up about 330 basis points on flat volume), and the reinforcing acquisition loop (buy at about 7x EBITA, valued at about 19x, with mix lifting each time) works above EBITA. But operating leverage is moderate: overheads have stayed at 11.8% of sales, one point of organic growth adds about 1.8% to EBITA, and cost-out scope is small by design. Financial leverage is low and unused, and the lines below EBITA (amortisation, floating-rate interest, tax) drag, so the forecast EPS-to-revenue ratio is about 1.2 against a median of about 2. The ordinary mix plus real pricing power and two unexercised gears puts it in the high 50s, between the groups' 74 for economic strength and 47 for forecasts.

#6Forecast financials

Bottom lineThe forecasts give about 10% a year of dependable EPS growth; growth of 12% or more needs the acquisition step-up, which is not in the base case.

What drives the forecasts. Organic growth of about 3.5% in FY2028 and 3% a year thereafter; acquired growth of 5% to 5.5% a year at the self-funded pace of deals; and a margin gain of about 30 basis points a year, roughly 60% of it from mix and the margins of acquired companies and 40% from overhead absorption. The alternation in EPS growth (12%, 8%, 11%, 9%) is a calendar effect: FY2027 contains two Easters and FY2028 none.

Inference: how the forecasts measure against three tests of a strong earnings case.

Double-digit growth: at the threshold

EBITDA and EPS compound at about 10% a year. That rate needs nothing the business has not just achieved in a worse environment: EBITA grew 12% to 14% a year through eleven quarters of flat volume.

Higher growth or margins than the past: higher margin level, lower growth

Revenue grows more slowly than the six-year 11.6% a year, the margin gain slows from about 85 basis points a year to about 30, and EPS growth falls from 16% to 10%. The difference reflects the absence of a repeat of the FY2022 to FY2023 boom, not a newly emerged weakness.

Growth clearly above 10% requires the deal step-up

An extra SEK 1bn a year of acquisitions adds 2.5 to 3 points a year to EPS growth from its second year.

One input I would change. Hardall International, announced on 16 November after the model's inputs were last set, adds about SEK 170m of annual sales. Including Hardall raises FY2027 revenue growth from 8.2% to 8.5%, and growth in the two remaining FY2027 quarters to 10.9% and 9.2%. The effect is about 0.3% on every later revenue level and about SEK 0.03 on EPS, so the figures in this memo remain the model's as it stands.

Against the market. Our FY2027 revenue is 2.4% and our EBITDA 3.5% below consensus; for FY2028 we are level, and for FY2029 1.5% above. On each broker's own EPS basis, our EPS is below five of the six visible brokers in FY2027 and FY2028, by 3% to 12%. The headline consensus EPS for FY2027 (SEK 10.20, "+28%") blends reported and adjusted forecasts and should not be used.

Strongest counter-case

The forecasts may be too cautious: margins have beaten forecasts every year, and Addtech's normal organic growth was 6% or more. They may also be too generous: acquired growth of 5% needs acquisition spending to rise from about SEK 1.7bn to SEK 2.4bn a year, at an unchanged entry price, in a more contested market.

What would change my view

The tests set out in topics #1 and #2, and a tax or interest outturn at the March 2027 year end, reported in May 2027, that matches the brokers' lower assumptions.

Conclusion: the forecasts give dependable growth of about 10% a year, at the threshold of double digits and below the past, with the step to 12% or more resting on an acquisition step-up that is not in the base.

Score: 75, set by the Rater. Ten percent sits right on the B/C cut-off, so I place it at the floor of B. More than half the growth is bought (organic 3% to 3.5% against 5% to 5.5% acquired). The margin gain slows from about 85 to about 30 basis points a year, EPS growth falls from the past 16%, reported EPS grows only about 9%, and consensus EPS growth of 9.5% is at the 41st percentile.

#7Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

Bottom line: consensus has the right level and the wrong shape. Consensus needs organic growth of 6% to 7% in the second half of FY2027, against an expected 3% to 4%, and assumes no further deals, falling interest costs and a flat tax rate. Net revisions should therefore be down through May 2027 and up from July 2027.

Evidence: how consensus is built. Only one broker's model is visible, so the composition of the rest of consensus is inferred from its totals.

  • Second half of FY2027. Consensus revenue implies growth of about 14.6%, against 7.0% in the first half. Acquisitions supply about 6 points and currency 1 to 2 points. The remainder, organic growth of 6% to 7%, compares with 1% in the first half and my forecast of 3% to 4%.
  • The Energy business area is the hinge of the gap. Consensus has Energy sales growing about 14% in the second half after falling 3% in the first; DNB Carnegie has nearer 19%. Our base case has about 6%. On my arithmetic from the segment figures, Energy alone accounts for between a third and a half of the whole gap in organic growth between consensus and our base case.
  • FY2028. Consensus revenue growth of 7.1% contains no unannounced deals, so it implies organic growth of about 5%. We reach the same EBITDA from organic growth of 3.5% plus about four points of growth from acquisitions not yet made.
  • Below EBITA. The leading broker assumes net financial costs falling to SEK 165m by FY2029 (the model: SEK 325m) and a tax rate of 22.5% (the model: 23.7%, rising to 24.1%).

Inference: four revisions to FY2028 estimates should arrive in different directions and at different times over the next 18 months. Deals, as they close, add about 4% to revenue and EBITDA. Organic growth printing below the consensus assumption takes away about 2.5%. A firmer krona, if it comes, takes away 1% to 1.5%. Net, FY2028 EBITDA barely changes. Like-for-like EPS, however, ends 3% to 5% lower, because each deal brings amortisation and interest costs with it, and because the brokers' tax and interest assumptions must move towards what Addtech is reporting.

Guidance. Addtech has no guidance to raise, and the odds that it introduces any are under 5%.

Narrative: what is known is positive and already priced; what is not yet discussed is mostly mechanical and negative for six months. The market expects the organic acceleration, the Automation recovery, the tilt towards grid investment and more deals. The market has not discussed the Easter calendar for 2027, the blend of bases in consensus EPS, the earn-out comparison, the drift in tax and interest, or the target's cliff in May 2028. Two unknowns are favourable: the size of the June-quarter rebound, and cash conversion that is sounder than its "soft" reputation.

So what. The scope for net upgrades over 6 to 12 months is limited, and it arrives late. The first report with a positive skew against expectations is the July 2027 report. By then consensus estimates should have been rebased, the calendar turns helpful, and a year of deals will have accumulated.

Against the market. The research consensus is that estimates are positioned to move moderately higher. I disagree for the next two reports and agree beyond them.

Strongest counter-case. Organic growth of 5% or more in the February report would validate the brokers' shape for FY2027 and leave every acquisition as a pure addition to estimates. A krona that stays weak would remove one of my three subtractions.

What would change my view. Organic growth of 5% or more in the February report; or brokers cutting their second-half revenue in their previews, which would lower the bar before the report instead of after it.

Conclusion: the probability of net upgrades is skewed to the negative through May 2027 and to the positive from July 2027, so the scope for upgrades is real but six to nine months away.

Score: 35, set by the Rater. There is no guidance to raise, and under 5% odds that any is introduced. Consensus needs 6% to 7% second-half organic growth against an expected 3% to 4%, and assumes lower interest and tax, so like-for-like EPS is likely trimmed 3% to 5% (about -0.4 to -0.6 times revenue growth) through the February and May 2027 reports. Upgrades arrive only from July 2027, late in the window, and the narrative already holds the acceleration story. The figures' +4% three-month revision (75th percentile) records past deal adds, not scope. In line with the group's 38, it sits a little below IMCD's limited scope and above TT Electronics, whose revisions are flattered by one-offs.

#8Current momentum: guidance, estimates, narrative, technicals and peers

Bottom lineMomentum is weak on every measure: the share-price weakness is shared with the premium cohort, while the estimate weakness is Addtech's own.

Evidence.

  • Guidance momentum: none, while peers supply it (Diploma raised its guidance three times in 2026; Lagercrantz raised its margin and capital targets).
  • Estimate momentum: the weakest in Addtech's cohort. Viewforth's dashboard rates Addtech's sell-side momentum C, while Indutrade, Lagercrantz, OEM International, Bufab and Beijer Ref are all rated A. FY2028 EBITDA estimates are flat over one month and up 1% over three months; their 9% rise over twelve months is about the size of the deals closed plus currency.
  • Technical momentum: D. The shares are just below their 200-day moving average, down 5.5% over three months, and at the 30th percentile of relative strength.
  • Thematic momentum: D.
  • Peers. Lagercrantz, OEM International and Diploma are also rated D on technicals; Indutrade and Bufab, which began the year on depressed multiples, are rated B. The cohort's valuation premium to Swedish capital goods has narrowed to about 13%, against a five-year average of 21%.
  • Narrative. All six visible brokers rate the shares Buy, with a mean target price of SEK 383. Yet the share price has lost about three points of multiple since early October with estimates unchanged.

Inference. Momentum is weak on every measure. The technical weakness belongs to the premium compounders as a group; the estimate weakness is Addtech's own. Judged by the share price, investors are already more sceptical than the analysts. But what the share price has discounted is the cohort's yield problem, not the Addtech-specific mechanics of the next two reports (the Easter calendar, the earn-out comparison, and the drift in tax and interest).

The precedent that fits: a good organic print defends a premium multiple but does not lift it while yields rise. Lagercrantz reported 12% organic growth and returned 1.5% over twelve months, about the same return as Addtech with 2% organic growth. Both began on premium multiples as yields rose. Indutrade's 40% rally came from a depressed multiple. A good organic print should therefore be expected to defend Addtech's multiple, not to lift it, unless yields stop rising. The downside is not symmetric: Lifco fell 12% in a day on a miss in organic growth.

So what. Nothing in current momentum argues for urgency, and the asymmetry of share-price reactions means that, at an unchanged multiple, the February report carries more risk than reward.

Against the market. Where the brokers and the share price disagree, I side with the share price for the next six months.

Strongest counter-case. Washed-out momentum, with the multiple at the 1st percentile of its two-year range, is where turns begin, and after the October correction DNB Carnegie judges the yield spread attractive again.

What would change my view. Sell-side momentum moving to B or A, with the share price above a rising 200-day average while yields are stable.

Conclusion: current momentum is weak across guidance, estimates and technicals, with the technical weakness shared by the premium cohort and the estimate weakness specific to Addtech.

Score: 57, set by the Rater. The parts hold it mid-band. Guidance gives none (neutral). FY2028 EBITDA estimates are flat over one month and +1% over three, the weakest in the cohort, although the figures show +4% EPS over three months. All six brokers rate it Buy, but the price has lost three multiple points. The shares are just below the 200-day average and down 5.5% over three months, and peers are mixed: the cohort's estimates are strong, its technicals weak.

#9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts

Bottom lineAddtech's earnings are low-risk; its share price is not, because a three-point move in the multiple outweighs the whole adverse earnings case.

Simplicity. The forecasts are simple from revenue down: every step from revenue to EPS runs on disclosed sensitivities. They are not simple at the first link, which is how demand becomes organic growth and when. Nor are they simple in Addtech's reporting, which uses three EPS conventions, includes earn-out gains inside the company's own EBITA, and will be distorted by the calendar for three consecutive quarters.

Fragility of the earnings: low

Acquired growth continues in every scenario, local managers cut costs within one to four quarters, and no customer, supplier or unit is large. The only fall in EPS in seven years came in the pandemic year. I put a probability of about 70% on FY2028 underlying EBITA landing within 6% of the base case, and I put the range of likely EPS outcomes over 18 months (the earnings cone) at about -12% to +7%.

Fragility of the share price: high

The two-year-forward multiple has ranged from 20 to 45 times in five years, and the fall from today's multiple to the guideline alone is larger than the whole adverse earnings case. I judge that the cohort and bond yields set two-thirds to three-quarters of the multiple's level. That judgement rests on proxies, because the files hold no measured co-movement.

Suddenness and trackability of the risks.

Trackable and dated

Organic growth (the 2 February report), the record of completed deals (in real time), the Riksbank (February) and peer reports (late January).

Sudden

A control failure in one of the units: I put the odds at about one in ten over two years, at a cost of SEK 50m to 150m of profit and more in multiple, because the premium rests on trust in decentralised control and Addtech has no internal audit function. Also a short-seller report on any member of the cohort, or a peer's miss in organic growth.

Slow

Entry multiples for acquisitions drifting up; the 15% target's cliff in May 2028.

Sector precedent: these stocks give back value through the multiple quickly and earn it back slowly. In the 2022 rate shock, the cohort's forward enterprise-value multiple fell from about 35 to about 15 times in roughly twelve months, and Addtech's recovery took about fifteen months. Indutrade's share price halved on a stall in organic growth combined with a write-down.

The five judgements, with the arithmetic if each is wrong. EPS effects are on FY2028 EPS of SEK 11.66 unless stated.

  1. Exit multiple: one point of multiple is worth SEK 14 a share, and EPS does not move. Value at March 2028 is the exit multiple times FY2030 EPS of SEK 13.98, so one point of multiple is SEK 14.0 a share, or 4.4% of today's price. Between the five-year low of 20.4 times and today's 26.1 times, the total return to March 2028 runs from about -7% to +18%. Because the exit multiple moves value with no change in EPS, it ranks first.
  2. Organic growth two points different for a year: SEK 0.41 of FY2028 EPS. Two points on FY2027 revenue of SEK 24,565m is SEK 491m of sales. At an incremental margin of about 30%, the extra sales give SEK 147m of EBITA, 3.3% of the FY2028 figure, and after tax at 23.9%, SEK 112m, or SEK 0.41 a share. Free cash flow barely moves in the first year, because working capital absorbs about 20% of the extra sales (SEK 98m). The same percentage carries into FY2030 EPS: about SEK 0.5 a share of EPS, or SEK 10 to 13 a share of value.
  3. Deal pace SEK 1bn a year higher: SEK 0.31 of EPS in the first full year. At FY2026's ratio of purchase consideration to acquired sales (1.46), an extra SEK 1bn buys SEK 685m of sales, about 2.5 points of growth. At 6.8 times EBITA, it buys SEK 147m of EBITA. After interest of about SEK 37m and tax, it adds SEK 84m, or SEK 0.31 a share, in the first full year. On reported EPS the gain is about half (SEK 0.17), because roughly SEK 50m a year of new amortisation comes with the acquisitions. Three years at the higher pace lift leverage to about 1.6 to 1.7 times EBITDA, inside the ceiling of 2.0. If the pace slips by the same amount, the effects reverse. If the entry price is wrong: paying 8.5 times EBITA instead of 6.8 on SEK 2bn a year of spending buys SEK 59m less EBITA, SEK 0.17 a share for each year of deals, or about 3.6% of FY2030 EPS after three years.
  4. Margin flat in FY2028 instead of up 50 basis points: SEK 0.38 of EPS. 0.5% of FY2028 revenue of SEK 26,874m is SEK 134m of EBITA (3.0%). After tax it is SEK 102m: SEK 0.38 a share, and the same amount of free cash flow.
  5. The lines the company does not control: SEK 0.21 to 0.28 of EPS each. One point on interest rates costs SEK 57m after tax, SEK 0.21 a share. A 5% stronger krona costs SEK 98m of operating profit by translation, SEK 0.28 a share, with no economic damage. In the other direction, if the leading broker is right on both interest (SEK 240m) and tax (22.5%), our FY2028 EPS is SEK 0.39 (3.4%) too low.
The bear case on earnings is smaller than a three-point move in the multiple. Taken together, the adverse sides of judgements 2, 4 and 5 cost about SEK 1.3 a share of FY2028 EPS, or 11%; a three-point move in the exit multiple is worth 13.2% of value.

Against the market. The market treats Addtech as low-risk because its earnings are low-risk. I agree on the earnings, but I think the low-risk label hides where the risk has moved: into a multiple the company does not control, and into reported numbers that will mislead for two quarters.

Strongest counter-case. Low earnings risk is what ultimately anchors a multiple, and a holder with a three-year horizon need not care about the path.

What would change my view. A measured co-movement showing that Addtech's multiple responds to its own delivery more than I judge; or evidence of an earnings fragility I have missed, most plausibly in the recently acquired companies.

Conclusion: the forecasts are simple and low-risk from revenue down, while the share price is neither, because a three-point move in a yield-driven multiple outweighs the entire adverse earnings case.

Score: 61, set by the Rater. The earnings are low-risk: an 18-month EPS cone of about -12% to +7%, about 70% odds that FY2028 EBITA lands within 6% of the base, no customer or supplier of weight, and 1.4x leverage. The share price is not: two-thirds or more of the multiple, which has ranged from 20x to 45x in five years, is set by yields and the cohort, and the move to the guideline alone outweighs the whole adverse earnings case. The case also carries a sudden control-failure risk in a group with no internal audit (about one in ten) and three quarters of calendar-distorted reports. Between the groups' 56 and 58 and lifted slightly for the narrow earnings cone, it sits below OEM International's net-cash version of the same model and just above Banca Generali.

#10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Bottom lineThe stock is bottoming while the business turns up; the low point in expectations probably lies ahead, around the May 2027 report.

Evidence. Viewforth's dashboard rule places Addtech in the Bottoming phase. The three clocks give different readings:

The business: turning up

Orders exceed sales, Automation is recovering, the manufacturing index is above 53, and peers are already reporting faster organic growth.

The estimates: stalling, not yet rebased

Estimates are flat to slightly down over a month, with a second-half bar the business is unlikely to clear and a May report that will look weak.

The multiple: bottoming against recent history, mid-range against long history

The two-year-forward multiple is at the 1st percentile of its two-year range and the 15th of its five-year range, but the 51st of its ten-year range.

Inference. I agree with Bottoming as the label for the stock, with one refinement that matters for timing: the bottom in expectations is probably ahead, not behind. Estimates have not yet been cut, the second-half bar is not low, and the report most likely to disappoint optically is still six months away. Addtech's business has turned before the market's expectations have reset, which is the reverse of the usual order and the reason the three clocks appear to contradict one another.

The sequence I expect.

1. Now to May 2027: the Bottoming phase completes, as brokers trim second-half revenue and move their below-EBITA assumptions.
➜
2. July 2027 onwards: the stock turns up, if the June quarter prints as the calendar suggests and the pace of deals holds.
➜
3. Thesis broadening needs something new: acquired sales running above SEK 2bn a year, which would change the growth rate rather than merely confirm it.

So what. The Bottoming phase argues for a multiple in the lower part of the historical range for now. The phase analysis also tells the reader which evidence would move the stock into the next phase, and when that evidence can arrive.

Against the market. Brokers describe a stock about to accelerate, which is the Turning-up phase. The share price describes a stock that is stalling. I sit between the two: Bottoming, with a dated route out.

Strongest counter-case. On the ten-year view the multiple is at its median, so the current level may not be a bottom at all, but the middle of a de-rating from five years of high multiples. If yields keep rising, the Bottoming phase becomes a Stalling phase.

What would change my view. Estimates cut by 3% or more with the multiple holding would mark the bottom as in. A further fall in the multiple with estimates intact would say that the de-rating is about yields and has further to run.

Conclusion: the stock is bottoming while the business turns up, with the low in expectations most likely around the May 2027 report and the turn-up phase earliest from July 2027.

Score: 47, set by the Rater. I agree with Bottoming, both computed and in the memo, but the order of events is unfavourable. The business is turning (orders above sales, Automation recovering), while estimates have not been rebased and the low in expectations is probably ahead, around the May 2027 report, with any Turning up no earlier than July 2027. The multiple sits at the 1st percentile of two years but the 51st of ten. That is less advanced than Solid State's Bottoming-into-Turning and a little better than Linea Directa's improvement not yet in forecasts.

#11The fair multiple

The guideline. Viewforth's guideline fair multiple for the Bottoming phase is the 30th percentile of the stock's own ten-year history of the two-year-forward P/E: 21.6 times on the latest dashboard reading (the model uses 21.5 times). The guideline is 17% below today's 26.1 times.

My view: the guideline is prudent, not punitive, and sits at the low end of a fair range of about 21.5 to 25 times; my central expectation is about 23 to 24 times. Three pieces of evidence support that view.

  1. The guideline is what the base case is worth at a required return a little above 8%. As a cross-check, I value the model's forecasts with DNB Carnegie's own published parameters: growth for eight years, then a terminal multiple of 18.5 times. That terminal multiple comes from 4% terminal growth and a 16% return on equity at an 8% cost of equity, and I recalculate it at each required return. The arithmetic is mine, and rough:
    Two readings follow from the valuation grid. First, today's price is the base case at a 7.5% required return, or about 12% growth at 8%. Second, half a point on the required return is worth three multiple points or more, 12% to 18% of value: more than a year of earnings growth, and more than the whole adverse earnings case. That sensitivity is the claim that "the multiple is hostage to yields", expressed as a number.
  2. The guideline is where the modern Addtech has troughed, briefly. In the 78 month-ends since May 2020, the multiple has closed at or below the guideline once (October 2023, at 20.6 times) and within half a point of it twice (October 2022 and September 2023). Each visit lasted a month or two. The ten-year history that produces the 30th percentile is weighted by the years 2016 to early 2020, when Addtech traded mostly at 15 to 19 times as a smaller, lower-margin and more Nordic group.
  3. The guideline gives nothing for the acquisition option. At the guideline multiple, the funded acquisition step-up comes free.

Why not higher

The five-year median multiple of 29.5 times capitalised EPS growth of 16% at lower yields, and neither condition holds today. A company growing EPS at 10% as interest rates rise, in a Bottoming phase with forecasts about to be rebased, belongs in the lower half of its range.

Why not simply the guideline

As a stress value, the guideline is right. As a point estimate for one date 17 months away, it assumes the stock sits at a level at or below which it has closed in only one month of the last six and a half years.

So what. The two points of multiple between the guideline and my central view are worth about SEK 28 a share, 9% of today's price. That gap is the size of my disagreement with the guideline, and it is a disagreement about yields and the cohort, not about Addtech.

Against the market. The market pays 26 times. In my view, 26 times needs either a required return of 7.5% while risk-free rates are rising, or the acquisition step-up. I am below the market and above the guideline.

Strongest counter-case. From below: at zero interest rates before 2020, Addtech traded at 17 times, so the whole 2020s range may be the anomaly. From above: the cohort is now treated as an asset class of its own, and Addtech's record through eleven quarters of flat volume is the kind of evidence that earns a multiple.

What would change my view. Yields: a move of half a point either way in the ten-year euro swap rate moves my fair range by about three multiple points. And the acquisition step-up: once it is visible, the fair range rises to about 25 to 28 times, because the growth rate has changed.

Conclusion: the guideline of about 21.5 times is a sound, prudent anchor that equals the base case at a required return just above 8%, and I regard it as the low end of a fair range whose centre is about 23 to 24 times.

Score: 53, set by the Rater. I place it in the low part of the band because the median multiple is barely deserved. EPS growth has stepped down from 16% to about 10% in a Bottoming phase with estimates still to be rebased, and the memo's own fair range (21.5x to 25x, centre 23x to 24x) sits below today's 26.1x. The slightly cheap peer reading and a ten-year history weighted to a smaller, lower-margin group stop it going lower.

#12Total shareholder return

Bottom lineEarnings and dividends deliver about 11% to 12% a year; at the guideline multiple, the de-rating takes back all of that over 17 months and two-thirds of it over three years.

The return at the guideline fair multiple (the model, from SEK 316.20).
HorizonTotal returnAnnualisedValue per shareFrom dividendsFrom the multipleFrom earnings
To 31 March 2028 (about 17 months)-2.3%-1.7%SEK 309+2.6%-17.7%+15.5%
To 30 September 2029 (about 2.9 years)+11.6%+3.9%SEK 353+4.1%-17.7%+30.7%

How the 17-month return is built. At March 2028 the shares are valued at 21.5 times FY2030 EPS of SEK 13.98, which is SEK 301, plus SEK 8.20 of dividends. Earnings two years ahead grow 15.5% over the period, while the fall in the multiple from 26.1 to 21.5 times takes away 17.7%. The two effects multiply to -4.9%, and dividends add 2.6%. Over three years, the same single fall in the multiple is set against twice the earnings growth.

What drives the return.

Earnings: about 10% a year, dependable

Earnings growth is the dependable part, because the earnings cone in topic #9 is narrow.

Dividends: about 1.2% a year

There are no share buybacks beyond those covering options. Management prefers acquisitions, and at today's multiple the arithmetic supports that preference: a buyback earns under 4%, while a deal at 7 times EBITA earns about 11% after tax on day one.

The multiple: the swing factor

The exit multiple decides the return, as the table below shows (my arithmetic on the model's earnings).

What the exit-multiple table shows.

  1. The stock is worth about 11% to 12% a year before any change in the multiple. That return is earnings growth plus the dividend.
  2. A return of 20% a year needs a re-rating or higher earnings. The re-rating required is to about 29 times over 17 months, or 33 times over three years. With the same forecasts, a return of 20% a year follows from a share price of about SEK 240 at the guideline multiple, about SEK 260 at 23.5 times, and about SEK 290 at an unchanged multiple.
  3. The acquisition step-up alone does not close the gap to 20%. Three to four years of an extra SEK 1bn a year of acquisitions lift horizon earnings by about 7% to 8%, which at an unchanged multiple takes the three-year return to about 13% to 14% a year.
The next six months lean the wrong way. No dividend falls in the window, and earnings two years ahead grow about 5%, so at an unchanged multiple the six-month return is about +5%. If the de-rating to the guideline came early, before the earnings had grown, the interim loss would be about 14% (21.5 times EPS of about SEK 12.7). The model reaches the guideline multiple at March 2028 without specifying the path, and the events of the next six months make an early de-rating more likely than a late one.

Against the market. Broker target prices imply a return of about 20% in twelve months, which needs a multiple of 28 to 29 times. The October memo's entry level assumed a multiple near 27 times; the guideline assumes 21.5 times. On the same business, that one assumption about the multiple accounts for the whole difference between "about 20%" and "about zero" over the next 17 months.

Strongest counter-case. A multiple at the 1st percentile of its two-year range can revert quickly once yields stop rising: after the 2022 trough, Addtech's multiple rose from about 22 to 30 times in eight months.

What would change my view. Yields and the cohort's multiple, for the first driver; the record of completed deals, for the second. Nothing in the earnings base is likely to change my view much.

Conclusion: the return is about 11% to 12% a year from earnings and dividends, less whatever the multiple gives back, which at the guideline is all of it over 17 months and two-thirds of it over three years.

Score: 33, set by the Rater. About +4% maps to about 35. I move it down for a fat lower tail: a -7% return at the five-year-low multiple, a possible interim loss of about 14% if the de-rating comes early, and a next six months that lean the wrong way. The three-year check, +11.6% to +22% (about 4% to 7% a year), is modest, with earnings plus the dividend (11% to 12% a year) absorbed by the multiple.

#13Summary conclusion

Addtech is easy to admire and, today, hard to get paid for.

The business is among the most dependable in European industrials. Addtech is a self-funded acquirer of profitable niches, with pricing power proven through a two-year volume trough, returns on capital above 20%, low leverage, and EPS that has fallen once in seven years. Its operating environment is improving, its restructured units are recovering, and its balance sheet holds a funded option on faster growth.

Three things stand between the quality of the business and the return on the shares.

The price

Today's price capitalises about two points more annual EPS growth than the base case contains.

The estimates

Consensus expects more from the next two reports than the business is likely to deliver, and a calendar effect that no broker has yet written about will distort those reports.

The multiple

Bond yields, which have just turned up, set the multiple for the whole cohort of premium compounders.

None of these three obstacles is a flaw in the company, and all of them can be tracked. Addtech will very probably deliver its earnings. The open questions are what multiple those earnings will be capitalised at, and when consensus estimates will stop running ahead of what the business delivers. On present evidence, the skew turns favourable when any two of the four conditions in the summary hold: consensus estimates have been rebased (most likely by the May 2027 report, with the June-quarter rebound and a year of deals still ahead); the record of completed deals shows acquired sales clearly above SEK 2bn a year; bond yields have stabilised; or the multiple has already moved towards the guideline while the business has not changed.

The first test is the report on 2 February 2027
  • organic growth of 3% or more,
  • Energy sales up year on year,
  • gross margin at least flat,
  • the first-half inventory build reversing in cash flow,
  • and no new earn-out gain.

Passing the test confirms the base case. Only organic growth of 5% or more would change the case.

58Thesis's Change Forces' Strength

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 58, set by the Rater. A moderate external tailwind (61) and gently positive internal change (56) turn into forecast EPS growth of about 10% a year, about the Universe median and below the company's own past. Most of that growth is bought and the margin gain is slowing, so this is a mild net positive in the high 50s, short of the low-to-mid 60s where clearly positive inputs lift profits to median growth, because the largest force, the deal step-up, is not yet delivered.

77Foundations' Robustness

Foundations' Robustness: 77, set by the Rater. The franchise is top-quarter (76): benign fragmented niches, a proven acquisition advantage, ROIC at the 87th percentile, low leverage and earnings that have fallen once in seven years, with the stability and predictability Richard prizes. The delivery record (50) is the ordinary part, because the long run of beats has thinned to earn-out-assisted meets, and light governance holds it below the 80s.

72Setups' Fit/Crispness

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 72, set by the Rater. In substance the case fits 'Delivering - Serial Acquirer - Mechanical EPS Upgrader': self-funded deals at about 7x EBITA, brokers adding each deal as it closes, and about 4% to 5% a year of mechanical upgrades. Two current problems blur the fit: earn-out write-backs show recent acquired cohorts below plan, and organic growth lags peers. I set aside the memo's main reason for C (consensus too high for the next two reports), because that is timing and is judged in topics 7 and 12.

63Case Riskiness

Case Riskiness: 63, set by the Rater. From revenue down the earnings case is simple and its risks are paper cuts (cone about -12% to +7%, low leverage, diversified). But the equity outcome is dominated by a yield-driven multiple about 17% above the guideline, and there are an unaudited control risk and two quarters of misleading reported numbers. That sits a little above Richard's Arteche 60, because the multiple is mid-range rather than very high, and well below CVS's boring 80s.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
